claims.claim: Sort the cells in your body by size, from red blood cells up, and something odd turns up: each size class weighs roughly the same. (Hook, A4: what a viewer who leaves at second two takes away.)
claims.note: PNAS Results: 'a roughly similar fraction of total body mass is present in each logarithmic cell-size class (Fig. 4A)'; Conclusion: 'cell biomass is roughly independent of cell-size class'. The hook uses the paper's own hedge ('roughly', 'each'). Adversarial: Fig. 4B (male, linear) runs from about 0.2 to 7 kg per class, and the paper says variation outside the dip is 'within two orders of magnitude', on a log axis across seven orders; 'roughly' carries this only because it is the paper's word. At second two the viewer has heard only 'sort the cells in your body by size', which leaves nothing false. 'Your body' generalises from the paper's reference male, female and child, all 'broadly similar'; the dip exception follows in line 9.

claims.claim: A twenty twenty-three study combined over fifteen hundred published sources to estimate the body's cells, type by type, and sorted them by size.
claims.note: PNAS 120(39), published online 18 Sep 2023 (pub-date in XML 18 09 2023). Abstract: 'data drawn from >1,500 published sources'; Methods: 'more than 1,500 published sources for 400 known cell types across 60 tissue systems ... 1,264 cell groups'. 'Estimate' is the paper's verb ('to estimate cell mass, size range, and cell count'). Sorted by size: whole-body cell-size histogram (Fig. 3).

claims.claim: The smallest cells it sorted are red blood cells.
claims.note: Methods: bins begin 'at the lower bound of erythrocytes'; 'We ignored binning cells smaller than erythrocytes (blood platelets and the smallest haploid gamete cells)'. Results: 'only considers the distribution beginning at red blood cells (4 × 10−11 g)'. 'It sorted' correctly excludes platelets and sperm, which are smaller.

claims.claim: The biggest are muscle fibres, more than a million times heavier.
claims.note: Results: 'from a tiny red blood cell to a myocyte, more than a million-fold larger'; the distribution extends 'from red blood cells to the largest myocytes'; size is cell mass in g throughout. Cross-check: myocyte peak ~1e-4 g / 4e-11 g = 2.5e6; SI gives sartorius fibres ≈7e-4 g; the 26 octave bins reach 2.7e-3 g. 'More than a million' is a floor, so not overstated.

claims.claim: Now put those cells into size classes, each class twice as heavy as the one before.
claims.source_checked: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10523466/fullTextXML; PNAS SI Appendix (pnas.2303077120.sapp.pdf, from the Europe PMC supplementaryFiles bundle)
claims.note: The figure is right (Methods: 'bins increase by a multiplicative factor of 2 ... (octave size classes)'; SI: 'each larger size class twice as large as the adjacent smaller size class'), but the wording says the CLASS is twice as heavy. A listener can hear that the total weight of each class doubles, which is the opposite of the short's core claim (each class holds roughly the same weight) and of the source. Change to make the cells, not the class, twice as heavy, e.g. 'each class for cells twice as heavy as the one before' or 'each class holding cells twice as heavy as the last'.

claims.claim: Each time the size doubles, there are, on average, about half as many cells.
claims.note: Methods: 'power law with a slope near −0.97 with a 95% CI of −1.09 to −0.87' over octave bins. Per doubling: 2^-0.97 = 0.51 (CI 0.47 to 0.55), so 'about half'. 'On average' is needed and present: Fig. 3 binned points scatter about the fit, with two classes near 1e-5 g about an order of magnitude below the line.

claims.claim: So the small cells win on numbers, the big cells win on size, and the two cancel out.
claims.note: Results: 'an increase in size by a given factor is offset by a decrease in cell count by a similar factor'. Fig. 1: 'Cell counts are completely dominated by red blood cells, platelets, and tissue resident white blood cells, while cell biomass is dominated by muscle and fat'. 'Cancel out' = 'offset'; the CI of the slope includes -1, and the next line says 'roughly'.

claims.claim: Every class ends up holding roughly the same weight.
claims.note: As claim 1: 'a roughly similar fraction of total body mass is present in each logarithmic cell-size class'; 'cellular biomass is overall approximately evenly spread among cell-size classes'. The exception is stated in the very next line.

claims.claim: With one exception: a dip, between the fat cells and the muscle fibres.
claims.note: Results: 'prominent biomass peaks comprising adipocytes (near 10−6 g) and myocytes (near 10−4 g), separated by a gap of relatively low biomass' and 'With the exception of this gap, all variation in cellular biomass lies within two orders of magnitude'. The paper singles out this gap as the one exception within the binned range (the other irregularities it names, around platelets and sperm, lie below the binned range). Fig. 4B shows the dip near 1e-5 g in all three bodies.

claims.claim: In a typical woman the dip is smaller, and in a typical ten-year-old it is fainter still.
claims.note: Results: 'This gap is also evident but less prominent in the reference female, and is even less evident in the 10-y-old reference child (Fig. 4B ...)'. 'Typical' = the paper's 'representative' reference models (female 60 kg, child 32 kg, 10 y). Note the female and child models are scaled from the male model (Approach), which the SOURCES entry records.

claims.claim: Take a typical man. His muscle fibres are fewer than one in fifty thousand of his cells with a nucleus.
claims.note: Fig. 1 caption (reference male): skeletal myocytes 'make up <0.002% of the nucleated cell count'. 0.002% = 1/50,000, and '<' is kept as 'fewer than'. 'Muscle fibres' is read as skeletal muscle fibres, the usual meaning and the paper's 'muscle fibers' (Significance); cardiomyocytes and smooth muscle cells are not in the figure. 'Typical man' = 70 kg reference male.

claims.claim: Yet they make up about half the weight of all his cells.
claims.note: Fig. 1 caption: 'Cell biomass is dominated by skeletal myocytes, comprising about half of all 45 kg of cell biomass'; 'remaining 23.5 kg' gives 21.5 kg (48%). SI: 'slightly less than 22 kg of myocyte mass'.

claims.claim: And all his cells together weigh about forty-five kilograms.
claims.note: Fig. 1 caption: '45 kg of cell biomass'. SI: 'giving a total of ~44.3 kg of cell mass'. 'About' covers both.

claims.claim: The other twenty-five of his seventy are not cells at all. They are the water, protein and minerals between them.
claims.note: Fig. 2 caption: 'noncellular components of biomass in each tissue, made up of extracellular water, protein, and minerals (~25 kg)'. SI: 'The remaining mass in the 70 kg male resides in extracellular content, including water (18 – 19 kg), protein (~3.7 kg), and minerals (~3.3 kg, most of which are bone minerals)', which sums to 25-26 kg. 'Between them' = extracellular. Reference male is 70 kg (Methods).

claims.claim: Sort the life in the ocean by size, as it was before industrial fishing, and most size classes held about the same weight too.
claims.note: Abstract: 'biomass within most order of magnitude size classes is indeed remarkably constant, near 1 gigatonne (Gt) wet weight ... but bacteria and large marine mammals are markedly above and below this value'. Evaluated in a 'pristine' state, 'before industrial-scale human capture of fish and marine mammals (pre-1850)'; today 'human impacts appear to have significantly truncated the upper one-third of the spectrum', so the past tense and 'before industrial fishing' are needed and present. 'Most' is the paper's word. Caveat for the record: the headline result is the upper 200 m; over the full depth bacteria and a mesopelagic-fish hump (0.01-1 g) stand higher, and the paper 'hesitate[s] to draw a strong conclusion' on the latter.

claims.claim: And in your body, nobody knows why. No accepted process explains it yet.
claims.note: Discussion: 'To our knowledge, there is no universally recognized process that accounts for these patterns'; Conclusion: 'the developmental mechanisms underlying this pattern remain unresolved'. The paper offers candidates (random growth; growth/division mismatch) without claiming them, so 'no accepted process' matches. 'Yet' is a 2026 claim resting on a 2023 source; a web search on 19 Nov 2026 found no later work claiming an accepted explanation (not an A2 source, so this only fails to break it).

claims.claim: Trillions of tiny cells, far fewer giant ones, and roughly the same weight at every size.
claims.note: Fig. 1 caption: nonnucleated blood cells ≈29 trillion of ≈36 trillion (plus ≈7 trillion nucleated). Muscle fibres <0.002% of nucleated cells. 'Roughly the same weight at every size' restates the paper's 'cell biomass is roughly independent of cell-size class' (Conclusion); the dip was stated two lines earlier.

claims.claim: Keyword card: "ROUGHLY THE SAME" (hook)
claims.note: As claim 1; the paper's 'roughly similar fraction ... in each logarithmic cell-size class'.

claims.claim: Keyword card: "1,500+ SOURCES"
claims.note: '>1,500 published sources' (Abstract), 'more than 1,500 published sources' (Methods).

claims.claim: Keyword card: "RED BLOOD CELLS"
claims.note: As claim 3: binning begins at the lower bound of erythrocytes.

claims.claim: Keyword card: ">1,000,000× HEAVIER"
claims.note: As claim 4: 'more than a million-fold larger', size measured as mass.

claims.claim: Keyword card: "×2 EACH CLASS"
claims.note: Same ambiguity as claim 5: '×2 EACH CLASS', shown while the line says the class is 'twice as heavy', reads as the class's weight doubling, which the source contradicts. Name what doubles, e.g. '×2 CELL SIZE EACH CLASS' or 'CELLS ×2 HEAVIER EACH CLASS'.

claims.claim: Keyword card: "HALF AS MANY"
claims.note: As claim 6: slope -0.97 gives 0.51× per doubling. The spoken 'on average' carries the hedge.

claims.claim: Keyword card: "THEY CANCEL OUT"
claims.note: As claim 7: 'offset by a decrease in cell count by a similar factor'.

claims.claim: Keyword card: "ABOUT THE SAME"
claims.note: As claim 8.

claims.claim: Keyword card: "ONE DIP"
claims.note: As claim 9: 'With the exception of this gap'.

claims.claim: Keyword card: "TYPICAL WOMAN"
claims.note: As claim 10: the 60 kg reference female, a 'representative' model.

claims.claim: Keyword card: "A TYPICAL MAN", sub "70 KG (154 LB)"
claims.note: Methods: 'Male, (70 kg, 176 cm ...)'. Recomputed 70 × 2.20462 = 154.3 lb, so 154 LB is right.

claims.claim: Keyword card: "< 1 IN 50,000"
claims.note: '<0.002% of the nucleated cell count' = fewer than 1 in 50,000; the '<' is kept.

claims.claim: Keyword card: "ABOUT HALF"
claims.note: As claim 12: 'about half of all 45 kg of cell biomass'.

claims.claim: Keyword card: "45 KG", sub "99 LB"
claims.note: '45 kg of cell biomass'. Recomputed 45 × 2.20462 = 99.2 lb, so 99 LB is right.

claims.claim: Keyword card: "NOT CELLS", sub "25 KG (55 LB)"
claims.note: 'noncellular components ... (~25 kg)'. Recomputed 25 × 2.20462 = 55.1 lb, so 55 LB is right.

claims.claim: Keyword card: "BETWEEN THE CELLS"
claims.note: 'extracellular water, protein, and minerals'.

claims.claim: Keyword card: "THE OCEAN TOO"
claims.note: As claim 15. The PNAS paper itself draws the parallel ('bodies in the ocean from bacteria to whales (44)').

claims.claim: Keyword card: "NOBODY KNOWS WHY"
claims.note: As claim 16: 'no universally recognized process', 'mechanisms ... remain unresolved'.

claims.claim: Keyword card: "NOT YET EXPLAINED"
claims.note: As claim 16.

claims.claim: Keyword card: "ROUGHLY THE SAME" (closing)
claims.note: As claims 1 and 17.

claims.claim: Chart, reference man: axis "CELL MASS IN GRAMS · LOG SCALE" from 10⁻¹¹ to 10⁻² g, with marks "RED BLOOD CELLS / FROM 4 × 10⁻¹¹ g", "FAT CELLS / ~10⁻⁶ g", "MUSCLE FIBRES / ~10⁻⁴ g"
claims.where: on-screen: size chart axis and marks
claims.note: 'red blood cells (4 × 10−11 g)' as the start of the distribution, 'adipocytes (near 10−6 g) and myocytes (near 10−4 g)'. Axis range covers the binned span (4e-11 to 2.7e-3 g); Fig. 3/4 axes are log, as labelled. 'FROM' correctly marks 4e-11 g as the lower bound, not a typical red-cell mass.

claims.claim: 26 size classes, each twice the mass of the last, starting at 4 × 10⁻¹¹ g
claims.note: Methods: 'bins increase by a multiplicative factor of 2 ... beginning at the lower bound of erythrocytes, and giving 26 size classes'; Fig. 3 caption '26 logarithmic size classes'. 4e-11 × 2^26 = 2.68e-3 g, inside the 10^-2 axis end and consistent with the Fig. 3 rightmost bin.

claims.claim: Bars "NUMBER OF CELLS · LOG SCALE · SCHEMATIC": a straight falling staircase
claims.note: The schematic contradicts the weight bars shown next to it and the paper's Fig. 3. Weight per class = count × cell mass, so the dip the weight bars show between fat and muscle must also appear as a dip in counts; in Fig. 3 the binned counts near 1e-5 g fall about an order of magnitude below the fitted line. A perfectly straight staircase implies level weight everywhere, with no dip. 'SCHEMATIC' covers simplification, not internal contradiction. Fix: draw the same dip in the count staircase at the same classes as the weight dip (keeping 'SCHEMATIC'), or relabel it as the fitted trend, e.g. 'AVERAGE TREND · LOG SCALE · SCHEMATIC'.

claims.claim: Bars "WEIGHT IN EACH CLASS · LOG SCALE · SCHEMATIC": roughly level, with a dip between the fat and muscle marks
claims.source_checked: Fig. 4 image (pnas.2303077120fig04.jpg) from the supplementaryFiles bundle; https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10523466/fullTextXML
claims.note: Fig. 4A (log axis) shows binned biomass near-level with a clear low between the adipocyte (~1e-6 g) and myocyte (~1e-4 g) peaks; Fig. 4B shows the same dip for the male. Labelled schematic, so smaller wobbles (and the low last class) need not be drawn. Fig. 4A plots the female; the paper says the male is 'broadly similar', and Fig. 4B confirms the male dip.

claims.claim: Text card "THE DIP BETWEEN FAT AND MUSCLE": "TYPICAL MAN: MOST PROMINENT", "TYPICAL WOMAN: SMALLER", "TYPICAL 10-YEAR-OLD: FAINTER STILL"
claims.note: 'This gap is also evident but less prominent in the reference female, and is even less evident in the 10-y-old reference child' implies the male is most prominent of the three. Text-only, so no linear-vs-log misdrawing.

claims.claim: Grid of 250 × 200 dots captioned "50,000 CELLS WITH A NUCLEUS · FEWER THAN 1 MUSCLE FIBRE", with one dot ringed
claims.note: 250 × 200 = 50,000 and the caption is right ('<0.002%'). But the ringed whole dot shows exactly one muscle fibre among 50,000, which the caption beside it says is not reached. The visual contradicts its own caption. Fix one of the two: caption 'AT MOST 1 MUSCLE FIBRE' (true, since '<' implies '≤') with the ringed dot, or keep 'FEWER THAN 1' and draw the ringed dot partly filled or faded so it reads as less than one.

claims.claim: Bar "ALL HIS CELLS · 45 KG", half of it filled and labelled "MUSCLE FIBRES ≈ HALF"
claims.note: 45 kg cell biomass, skeletal myocytes 'about half' (21.5 kg = 48%; SI 'slightly less than 22 kg'). A half fill with '≈' is within drawing precision.

claims.claim: Bar extends with "NOT CELLS · 25 KG", label "70 KG MAN" and "WATER · PROTEIN · MINERALS"; lengths drawn 45:25
claims.note: Fig. 2 caption '~25 kg' extracellular water, protein and minerals; SI water 18-19 kg + protein ~3.7 kg + minerals ~3.3 kg; 45 + 25 = 70 kg reference male. Proportional lengths, so no scale distortion.

claims.claim: Ocean card: axis "SIZE OF SEA LIFE, BACTERIA TO WHALES · LOG SCALE", level bars titled "BEFORE INDUSTRIAL FISHING · SCHEMATIC"; first three bars higher, last two lower
claims.note: Fig. 2B (upper 200 m, linear) read directly: the first three bins stand at about 2.5, 2.5 and 1.9 Gt, the middle bins near 1 Gt (fish ~0.8), and the last two (mammal) bins near 0.1 Gt or below, so 'first three higher, last two lower' matches. Axis is log body mass (g) in the paper, from bacteria to whales; 'pristine ... (pre-1850)' matches the title. For the record: this is the paper's upper-200 m spectrum; over the full depth the bacterial bins and a mesopelagic-fish hump rise further, and the card does not say which. Covered by 'SCHEMATIC' and by the paper's headline framing.
